[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Transactions, Concurrency, and Locking in Ruby on Rails"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When building robust web applications with Ruby on Rails, data integrity is paramount. As traffic grows, multiple users or background jobs will inevitably attempt to read and modify the same database records simultaneously. Without proper concurrency control, this leads to race conditions, lost updates, and corrupted data."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding Database Transactions"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A database transaction wraps multiple SQL statements into a single unit of work following the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). In Rails, ActiveRecord provides a simple way to manage transactions using ActiveRecord::Base.transaction."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"Account.transaction do
  sender.withdraw(100)
  receiver.deposit(100)
end"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"If any exception occurs within the block, the entire transaction is rolled back, and database changes are undone. If the block finishes successfully, the transaction is committed."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"The Concurrency Problem"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Transactions alone do not solve concurrency issues if two operations overlap in time. Imagine two users reading an item's inventory count (which is 10) at the exact same millisecond. User A decrements it by 2 and saves it (8). User B decrements it by 3 and saves it (7). The correct inventory should be 5, but because of the race condition, User A's update was lost."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Pessimistic Locking"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Pessimistic locking assumes that conflicts are likely to happen. It locks the database record as soon as it is read for update, preventing other transactions from modifying or locking the record until the current transaction is finished."},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"In ActiveRecord, you implement pessimistic locking by calling lock on a relation using SQL's FOR UPDATE clause."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"Item.transaction do
  item = Item.lock.find(1)
  item.inventory -= 1
  item.save!
end"},{"order":13,"bullet_point":"Pros: Guarantees absolute safety against race conditions."},{"order":14,"bullet_point":"Cons: Reduces concurrency performance, can cause deadlocks, and increases database wait times."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Optimistic Locking"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Optimistic locking assumes that conflicts are rare. Instead of locking database rows, it checks whether another process has modified the record since it was last read. ActiveRecord achieves this by using a integer column namedlock_version on the table."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"class AddLockVersionToProducts < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  def change
    add_column :products, :lock_version, :integer, default: 0, null: false
  end
end"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you update a record with optimistic locking, Rails automatically increments the lock_version and adds a check to the SQL UPDATE statement ensuring the version matches."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"product = Product.find(1)
# Another process updates product, incrementing lock_version to 1
product.name = 'Updated Name'
product.save! # Raises ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"If a stale object error is raised, your application must handle it gracefully, usually by reloading the record and prompting the user to merge changes."},{"order":21,"bullet_point":"Pros: High concurrency, no database locks held, great for web applications with heavy read traffic."},{"order":22,"bullet_point":"Cons: Fails fast on conflict, requiring retry logic or user intervention."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Choose pessimistic locking when write conflicts are frequent and data correctness is strictly critical (e.g., financial transactions). Choose optimistic locking for standard web forms and collaborative editing where conflicts are infrequent."}]
